corpus.title: Germany is electing far-right and socialist parties. What does it mean for the country's floundering centre?
corpus.signal_text:
Germany is electing far-right and socialist parties. What does it mean for the country's floundering centre?
Growing polarization marks unstable future for mainstream politics and German chancellor
Right after the election results came in Sunday night, Germany’s chancellor stood in front of journalists and described it bluntly: "Es ist ein disaster." ("It is a disaster.")
Friedrich Merz’s centre-right party, the Christian Democratic Union (CDU), has suffered catastrophic losses in a number of recent regional elections.
Over the weekend in the state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the CDU had its worst performance in history, failing to win enough votes to even keep a seat in the legislature. The far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) came in first place — for the second time in just a few weeks.
In the city state of Berlin, the CDU was unseated from the other side of the political spectrum by the democratic socialist Die Linke ("The Left").
The CDU has been the most dominant party of Germany's postwar history. The fact that more Germans now say in surveys that they'd rather vote for a far-right party marks a seismic shift.
For a political system designed for stability, the rise of both the far-right and hard-left signals a crisis for the country's mainstream politics.
"People are getting polarized more and more these days," said Leonie Siwter, a Die Linke supporter who was celebrating at the Berlin watch party on Sunday night.
"In the last few years, our Chancellor Merz has managed with every single announcement to make himself less and less popular," she said. "They’ve lost a lot of trust."
On Sunday, Merz vowed to stay in his role but will do so on increasingly shaky ground, with his approval rating sitting at 13 per cent — a record low.
Elections in Germany's 16 states don't directly impact Merz's job. But his party's poor regional results challenge his viability as the country's national leader.
Disillusion with the mainstream
Like other democracies, Germany is seeing the rise of a far-right, nationalist movement — and in many ways, a radical left in response.
"The biggest part why people are voting for the Left Party now is because they’re afraid of the right parties and fascism growing in Germany," Die Linke supporter Michael Berger told CBC News.
